name: Dana Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and supervise four people who gather food-safety records for a large restaurant chain. We check temperature logs, chase missing supplier labels and prepare a report when a site has a problem. I use AI every day to flag odd entries and draft a first report, though my senior clerk still catches mistakes I miss. I like finding a bad batch before it reaches a customer; I hate getting a call from a kitchen after I signed off too early.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How new are you to management, and what is at stake at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I only took this junior manager job nine months ago after finishing a bachelor’s degree years earlier. My husband, Aaron, drives a bus; our children are ten and fifteen, and we have a mortgage. My pay is about normal for this role, with about five months of expenses saved, and some similar offices are nearby. I try technology early but make myself check the source record, because my family needs the job and the kitchen needs a true answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say keep the useful flagging tool, but a person should read the original temperature sheet before closing a case. A kitchen cannot cook safely from a guessed number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job should stay and our five-month reserve gives us room for an ordinary surprise. Aaron’s driving pay is steady, so I would use the time to become a better manager rather than chase a new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep checking each flagged cold-storage log against the paper sheet and ask the senior clerk to review my weekly report. During the first year Aaron and I would keep moving 140 a month into emergency savings while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our work and home budget. The software saving a few minutes would be fine, but it would not decide food safety for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a false cold-storage alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would phone the kitchen and check the original reading before stopping a delivery. A false alarm can waste food, while a missed warm fridge can make someone ill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does asking the clerk to review your report bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, because I’m meant to be the manager. I would rather learn my senior clerk’s checks than protect my pride with a wrong sign-off.

A useful flag still needs a **human safety decision**.
think: My **job looks stable** in a plateau.

Transfer **140 monthly** into savings while both wages hold.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and home money.

steps.text: Keep checking flagged cold-storage logs against original temperature sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell kitchens that software will write reports and check logs, but it needs a test against actual bad batches. I’d ask our director to say how many record-checking jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small team could be combined with another manager’s when routine checks disappear, and I’m the new one here. I’m quick with software, but I still rely on my clerk to catch judgment errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d test the new checker on sixty closed safety cases and count missed warm-fridge readings. In the first year I’d complete the paid site-inspection course our firm offers, then apply for posted field audit shifts only if the pay stays near my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because I might help build the thing that cuts my own post. I still want to know whether it really catches unsafe food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would see the results before a rollout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchens and our records team should see both false alarms and missed cases. I would not call a tool safe just because it makes clean charts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the field audit shifts pay less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep asking about other posted work and stay in my current job while I can. Our mortgage is not paid by an interesting job description.

Management should publish the **remaining record posts**.
I’d share **missed-case counts** with the kitchens before rollout.
think: A combined team might remove **my junior manager job**.
My clerk still catches **judgment errors** that speed cannot fix.
do: Test **sixty closed cases** for missed warm-fridge readings.
Complete a **paid site course** and seek field shifts only at viable pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own post.
S1.quote: Our mortgage is not paid by an interesting job description.
fieldNote: She measures the tool by **missed unsafe readings**.
Her daily AI skill does not erase **junior job risk**.
Field shifts require **paid training** and near-current wages.

steps.text: Test AI checks against sixty closed food-safety cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company must give record staff clear dates and written terms before closing a team. Kitchens need a person to call if a machine flags their stock incorrectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could do the checking and report writing I supervise, so I expect my post to go. Aaron’s bus driving may last until robots come around 2031, but one wage would not cover our mortgage and the younger child’s school costs for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Aaron and I would pause our planned car upgrade and keep its deposit in cash. Before 2028 I’d ask three local restaurant sites about paid on-site food checks and enroll in a safety certificate only if the company funds both the fee and study time; after AGI arrives, I’d take a posted site role only if its written wage covers our mortgage share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. Two years is short when both my desk work and, a few years later, Aaron’s driving income are in the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Aaron about his bus work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the robots in this picture arrive around 2031, so his driving pay may buy us time after my job changes. I would not call it a permanent plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the site roles are unpaid placements?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take one. A certificate and a free shift do not meet the mortgage payment.

Kitchens need a **human contact** for wrong stock flags.
think: Aaron’s bus wage may last until **2031 robots** but cannot carry us alone.
do: Pause the **car upgrade** and keep its deposit available.

feel: I feel **alarmed** about two income deadlines.
S2.quote: A certificate and a free shift do not meet the mortgage payment.
fieldNote: Her office work faces the **2028 thinking deadline**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets people finish a proper food-safety qualification while the company still pays them. I’d also ask managers to show which site vacancies actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into site visits before 2031 and keep earning while I learn. The reports and decisions in site inspection still face AGI in 2031; Aaron’s driving and physical checks face robots around 2034, so we need more than one backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d enroll in a company-funded food-safety qualification if the study hours are paid and Aaron can collect the younger child on late days. I’d shadow the kitchen audit team during two paid site visits, then apply for a posted site auditor role before 2031 only if the wage covers the mortgage; after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while the site keeps paying for human checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years lets me test the work before leaving my team. I can ask Aaron how late pickup fits his bus route instead of assuming he can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Aaron cannot cover pickup on those days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would move the course days or ask my older child only if that fits their school commitments. I will not make my older child run the household so I can chase a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid site visit show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I can spot a real storage problem without hiding behind the report. I need that practice before I sign a safety finding alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives employers time to offer proper apprenticeships and honest wage figures. Families should know when records jobs change before signing new loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child would be grown by 2036, but the mortgage and our younger child’s training costs may remain. I could build savings, move toward site work and encourage the younger one to try a paid apprenticeship instead of borrowing for a course with no job. Site reports and decisions would still face AGI in 2036, while physical checks and Aaron’s bus driving face robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Aaron and I would put 220 monthly into savings while both wages hold and the mortgage stays at its current payment. I’d complete a paid safety qualification if a site offers supervised shifts, apply for a posted audit role before 2036 only if it keeps our mortgage paid, and discuss paid apprenticeship adverts with our younger child; after AGI arrives, I’d stay in site work only while human checks are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but ten years gives the whole family time to make choices. I would not buy a new car before we know what happens to both paychecks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger child about their studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say look at the paid apprenticeship adverts alongside any college course, and ask what wage each route actually leads to. I would not decide my younger child’s training for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the site role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want a written wage, supervised shifts and actual inspections, not only a new title. The site’s reports and decisions face AGI in 2036, before robots reach hands-on checks around 2039. Aaron’s driving faces that later date too, so I would keep the savings account growing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my desk job could end before I have site practice, and Aaron’s driving income has its own later deadline. A paid qualification, supervised shifts and a real wage on a posted site job would help. I need a plan that keeps the mortgage paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who answers a kitchen when a machine labels good food as dangerous. A clean report is no comfort to the cook watching a delivery go in the bin.

headlineQuote: A clean report is no comfort to the cook watching a delivery go in the bin.
portrait: **Dana**, 43, is a new food-safety records manager with a bachelor’s degree.
Typical pay and **five months saved** support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses **AI daily** but checks flagged entries against original records.
She seeks **paid site training** while considering her husband’s later driving risk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her thinking-heavy records post before she gains site experience.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid qualification**, supervised shifts and a posted site role with a viable wage would help.
